slides.title: Principle and purpose
bullets: Urea is formed in the liver when ammonia is detoxified; its level in blood gives information about kidney function and protein metabolism.
Urease turns urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Ammonia, with α-ketoglutarate and NADH, is turned into L-glutamate with the help of glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH); NADH is used up.
The fall in absorbance at 340 nm is proportional to the amount of urea.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: Specimen: non-haemolysed serum; heparin plasma.
R1 — buffer (Pipes, pH 7.8) and α-ketoglutarate; R2 — substrate (urease, GLDH, NADH); R3 — urea standard 8.325 mmol/L (50 mg/dL).
Working reagent: one vial of R2 is dissolved in the required volume of R1 buffer, mixing slowly until fully dissolved.
Stability: 20 days at 2–8 °C, up to 5 days at room temperature.

slides.title: Specimen and reagents
bullets: The volumes, times and concentrations given belong to the kit named in the manual (Hospitex Diagnostics); with another kit follow its instructions.

slides.title: Procedure (manual)
rows: Mix; measure A1 after 30 seconds and A2 after 60 seconds; ΔA = A2 − A1
340 nm, 37 °C, 1 cm cuvette, zero — air or distilled water

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Urea (mmol/L) = sample ΔA / standard ΔA × standard concentration.
Linearity up to 49.8 mmol/L (300 mg/dL); samples with a higher concentration are diluted 1:4 with distilled water and the result multiplied by 5.
Reference in the manual (serum or plasma): 1.66–8.3 mmol/L (10–50 mg/dL); each laboratory applies its own reference range.

Raised: glomerulonephritis, chronic impairment of kidney function, obstruction of the urinary tract, rapid protein breakdown, dehydration, high-protein diet, febrile infections, diabetes mellitus, burns.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Lowered: a diet low in protein and carbohydrate, rapid protein utilisation (late pregnancy, children under a year), severe liver disease, chemical poisoning, malabsorption.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: If the working reagent is out of date or wrongly stored, NADH breaks down and the measurement is wrong.
The timing of the A1 and A2 readings (30 and 60 seconds) must be kept exactly.
A haemolysed or turbid sample may distort the result.
If the result is above the limit of linearity, dilute the sample and repeat.
Quality control: measure a control serum in every analytical series and record the result on the control chart.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Working reagent: one vial of R2 is dissolved in the required volume of R1 buffer, mixing slowly until fully dissolved; stable for 20 days at 2–8 °C and up to 5 days at room temperature.
Calibration: by standard — the kit R3 urea standard, 8.325 mmol/L (50 mg/dL); the concentration is given on the standard vial.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: Mode — fixed time: A1 is read after 30 seconds and A2 after 60 seconds; ΔA = A2 − A1.
Zero: against air or distilled water; 340 nm, 37 °C, 1 cm cuvette.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The values belong to the Hospitex Diagnostics kit and the Screen Master Plus photometer in the manual. The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the parameters against them.

slides.title: Semi-automatic analyser: urea programme
rows: By standard; the concentration is given on the standard vial

slides.title: Semi-automatic analyser: urea programme
rows: 8.3 / 1.6 (normal range in the method section: 1.66–8.3 mmol/L)

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Serum and plasma are potentially infectious: wear gloves; never pipette by mouth.
When handling kit reagents follow the warnings in the instructions.
Used cuvettes and tubes are disinfected.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: BUN is often part of a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) and helps diagnose or monitor kidney diseases. Because early kidney disease usually has no signs or symptoms, it is also used to screen people at risk.
BUN is often interpreted together with blood creatinine from the same panel (one of the test’s other names is BUN-to-creatinine ratio); this comparison can help find the cause of a kidney problem.

slides.title: Urea
slides.eyebrow: Kidney function · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: MedlinePlus covers this analyte as the BUN (blood urea nitrogen) test, which measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood. Urea nitrogen is a waste product formed as the body breaks down proteins; it is carried in blood and removed by the kidneys in urine.

slides.title: Urea
cols: A high BUN generally suggests that the kidneys are not working well. Other possible causes include dehydration, burns, certain medicines, a high-protein diet and a recent heart attack.
Possible causes of a low BUN include a lack of protein in the diet, malnutrition and liver disease.

slides.title: Urea
bullets: Pre-analytics: Usually no special preparation is needed. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting for several hours may be required.
Limitations: BUN levels vary with sex and usually increase with age. An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
BUN is only one measure of kidney function. If kidney disease is suspected, other tests may be needed, such as creatinine and GFR, which estimates how well the kidneys filter blood.
